name: Big Dipper
label: Homestead
lede: Bill Goffrier and Gary Waleik started on a Boston porch with songs left over from two broken-up bands, painted UFOs on their sleeves, and made one Epic album, Slam, with a cover they hated.

eras.title: Two bands fall apart, one porch fills up
eras.text: The Embarrassment wind down in Kansas, and Gary Waleik and Steve Michener leave Volcano Suns in Boston. Goffrier meets Waleik at a Suns show, they trade songs on a porch, and by spring 1986 they have demos and a deal but no name.

years.src: The College Crowd Digs Me · Wikipedia
years.h: Wichita's Embarrassment end, and Bill Goffrier enrols in art school in Boston
years.p: The band that mailed its own tapes around the world stopped when two members moved to Boston. Goffrier, the guitarist, went for graduate art studies.
years.xp:
The Embarrassment formed in Wichita, Kansas in 1979 and built a following with basement recording, tapes mailed to labels, college radio and constant touring. Goffrier says they opened for Iggy Pop, Public Image Ltd. and Pete Shelley, and never landed a major deal.

He told an interviewer he wasn't looking to start another band in Boston. A Volcano Suns show changed that.

years.src: Wikipedia · Rock Town Hall · The College Crowd Digs Me
years.h: Two Volcano Suns quit before the first album is out
years.p: Guitarist Gary Waleik and bassist Steve Michener leave drummer [[Peter Prescott|f69ea4d3-4065-49ff-b076-585bfc6e79ff]]'s band sixteen months in.
years.xp:
Prescott, late of [[Mission of Burma|db9d25d7-a85b-4a29-b2ff-8f5b69ed691e]], formed Volcano Suns in spring 1984. Wikipedia says he had auditioned for a drummer's spot in another band and took two of its members instead. Waleik says they "started to argue a lot, and it was no fun," and that everyone was better off for moving on.

Goffrier caught a Suns show in mid-1985 and got talking to Waleik, an Embarrassment fan. The songwriting sessions that followed, on a porch, became Big Dipper.

years.h: Goffrier and Waleik trade songs on a porch
years.p: Goffrier told an interviewer it wasn't a band at first. It was three people, Michener on bass, trading songs.

years.h: Gerard Cosloy offers Homestead's deal before the band has a name
years.p: Waleik mailed demos to Cosloy in May 1986 and got an unsolicited contract back.
years.xp:
Drummer Jeff Oliphant, Waleik's cousin, had played speed metal in XS. The six-song demo included "Faith Healer," which got regular college radio play.

Waleik calls the group an experimental pop band, drawing on the Soft Boys, the odder Beatles and the artsy end of punk and power pop.

eras.title: Homestead's flying saucers, then Epic's click track
eras.text: A UFO painting fronts Heavens and a Swiss farmer's Pleiades story turns up on Craps, all on Homestead. Epic signs the band in 1989, and by 1992 it's over.

years.cap: Flyer for Big Dipper and Bone Ranger at Finale's, Boston, Sunday Oct. 25, c. 1987
years.src: The College Crowd Digs Me · Music Museum of New England
years.h: The Mekons are on the bill for Big Dipper's first show, at The Rat
years.p: Goffrier remembers the debut as a support slot at Boston's Rat. A later flyer has the band headlining Finale's, billed "From Boston on Homestead Records."
years.xp: The Rat, on Kenmore Square, was Boston's basement rock room. Big Dipper became a Boston regular after this, and the Music Museum of New England lists the Rathskeller and the Channel among their local haunts.

years.h: Boo-Boo is the first record, and "All Going Out Together" gets a 12-inch
years.p: Homestead puts out the EP in 1987; Demon Records handles the UK.

years.cap: Flyer for Big Dipper at the Grand Emporium, Kansas City, Monday Feb. 22
years.src: Wikipedia · Rock Town Hall · Music Museum of New England
years.h: Paul Q. Kolderie produces Heavens; Goffrier paints the sleeve
years.p: The UFO on the cover is Goffrier's. AllMusic calls the album one of the finest American indie records of its era.
years.xp:
Waleik says Heavens was the peak of the first run: they spent months writing and rehearsing, and "couldn't wait to record that album."

"Mr. Woods" was covered by Gigolo Aunts on a 1996 benefit compilation. NME gave the record 5 out of 10 at the time.

Goffrier's old Kansas stomping ground turned up on the touring calendar too: a flyer has Big Dipper at Kansas City's Grand Emporium on Monday, Feb. 22, with Shotgun Solution and Naked Prey.

years.cap: CBGB calendar flyer listing Big Dipper with the Pixies, Friday Mar. 25, c. 1988
years.src: Wikipedia · Rock and Roll Globe · Music Museum of New England
years.h: A Swiss UFO contactee gets a whole song on Craps
years.p: "Semjase" is about Billy Meier, the Swiss farmer who claimed contact with beings from the Pleiades. The band called the record a pop album.
years.xp:
The Boston Globe praised its "winsome, off-center melodies" and hooks. It closes the Homestead contract; Rock and Roll Globe describes Craps as the end of a three-album deal.

"Ron Klaus Wrecked His House" outlived everything else here: in 2016 it was used in the film Gold, and it appears on the soundtrack.

A CBGB flyer from the same stretch lists Big Dipper with the Pixies on Friday, March 25.

years.big: "We signed too early. We were ahead of our time."
q: We signed too early. We were ahead of our time.
years.h: Big Dipper signs to Epic, before the alternative gold rush
years.p: Steve Michener, looking back. Their management pushed the deal, the band says, on the argument that they'd done all they could on a small label.
years.xp: Epic signed four indie-leaning bands at once: Big Dipper, O Positive, Social Distortion and the Rave-Ups. Michener says management "bought into this idea that we were worthy of being on a major label." Once Social Distortion took off, he says, the label lost interest in the rest.

years.src: Rock and Roll Globe · Wikipedia · The Agit Reader · The New York Times
years.h: Epic's Slam puts horns and samples on a click track
years.p: Recorded in North Carolina with Steve Haigler, the Epic debut has 14 songs and closes on a cover of Mott the Hoople's "All the Way from Memphis."
years.xp:
Michener says they split the sessions into four phases by style, taking a cue from Beatles recording histories, and played to a click track for the first time. The New York Times ran a feature titled "Big Dipper Combines Punk With Melody" in April 1990.

The Boston Globe found the band in fine form; The Village Voice gave it a C+. Waleik says a few songs are wonderful but the record is not a good one.

years.h: Epic shows the band a Slam sleeve they hadn't picked
years.p: The label hired professionals and spent real money, then handed over a cover the band disliked. Told it was too late to change, Goffrier calls it the major-label experience in a nutshell.
years.xp:
Michener is harsher, calling the cover "basically unforgivable" and his least favorite part of the whole record.

Because Epic (Sony) owns the master, the band can't reissue Slam without Sony's permission. They needed it just to include one demo on Supercluster.

years.src: Rock and Roll Globe · The Agit Reader
years.h: Michener works out his exit over lunch at Nosmo King
years.p: The Slam tour is winding down around a July show at New York's Marquee when he and Waleik settle it at the restaurant.
years.xp:
Goffrier says the label "really didn't care at all about us" and that it was discouraging. Tom Brewitt took over on bass, according to The Agit Reader.

The video is a full show from June 16, 1990, a month before Michener leaves.

years.h: Epic drops the band, and a 7-inch turns up on Feel Good All Over
years.p: Within about a year of Slam, per Wikipedia and the Music Museum of New England. The 7-inch is "Approach of a Human Being."
years.xp: Waleik, looking back: "we never really recovered from the Epic experience."

years.h: Two more years, then Waleik stops
years.p: After Michener left he carried on for two years with Goffrier, then walked away.
years.xp: The band had been working with session players and left unreleased material, which resurfaced on the third disc of the 2008 anthology.

eras.title: A box set, a reunion, one more album
eras.text: Merge's Supercluster gets the band back onstage in 2008. In 2012 comes a new record, 22 years after Slam, from a label that wanted them.

years.cap: Goffrier, Waleik, Oliphant and Michener, c. 2008
years.h: Merge puts out Supercluster, with Tom Scharpling on the intro
years.p: Boo-Boo, Heavens and Craps, remastered, plus 15 unreleased songs from after Slam. Scharpling hosts The Best Show.
years.xp: Pitchfork gave the anthology 7.8 out of 10. Waleik credits Scharpling's persistent campaigning, from 2004, for the reunion: "Tom certainly got the ball rolling," he says.

years.cap: Steve Michener, Jeff Oliphant, Goffrier and Waleik at Midway Cafe, Boston, April 2008
years.h: Big Dipper is back onstage the month after the box set
years.p: Wikipedia dates the first reunion performances to April 2008, and a photo from the Midway Cafe stage has Michener and Oliphant back with Goffrier and Waleik.

years.cap: Waleik and Steve Michener swap instruments for "Sam Hill," Midway Cafe, Boston
years.h: Rock Band players can download "All Going Out Together"
years.p: "She's Fetching" and "Younger Bums" go into the game as downloadable tracks too.

years.cap: Big Dipper at the Middle East, Cambridge, Massachusetts
q: Almost Ready was the only label we could find that had any confidence in us.
years.src: The Agit Reader · Beats Per Minute · The Rumpus
years.h: After 22 years, Crashes on the Platinum Planet
years.p: Almost Ready Records puts it out in November. Over four years the band had convened only sporadically to record.
years.xp:
Waleik produces NPR's Only a Game and Goffrier teaches art in Boston; Michener is a nurse in Oregon and Oliphant works in finance.

Robert Pollard of Guided by Voices, an early fan, once told Waleik he thought Big Dipper were the 20th best rock band ever, Waleik says.
